specPoints.text: describe an experiment to prepare a pure, dry sample of a soluble salt, starting from an insoluble reactant

primer.text: From Bases you already know that metal oxides and hydroxides neutralise acids to form a salt and water. This note turns that chemistry into a working method: how to prepare, purify and crystallise a soluble salt starting from an insoluble base.

lessons.title: Prepare a soluble salt
lessons.opening: A soluble salt can be made by warming an acid with an insoluble base such as a metal oxide. The base is added until some of it is left over, which guarantees the acid has all reacted, and the leftover solid is then filtered away. What remains is a solution of the salt alone, ready to be concentrated and crystallised.
keyPoints: A soluble salt forms when an acid reacts with an insoluble base.
The insoluble base is added in excess so that all of the acid reacts.
Filtration removes the excess solid, leaving only the salt and water in solution.
Heating evaporates water until small crystals begin to appear, usually when about half the water has gone.
Slow evaporation over several days lets larger crystals grow.

low.restatement: Warm the acid with the insoluble base and keep adding base until a little of it stays solid, which proves the acid is used up. Filter the extra solid away, then heat the clear solution so that water leaves and crystals of the salt begin to appear.
low.analogy: It works like pouring sugar into tea until no more dissolves: the undissolved spoonfuls at the bottom prove the drink is full, and you simply filter or scoop the surplus out before drinking.
low.examPointer: Method questions award marks in order, so write react, filter, evaporate and crystallise as separate steps rather than one sentence.

medium.restatement: The insoluble base sits in excess precisely so that every trace of acid is used up, because surviving acid would concentrate dangerously as the water evaporates. Once the surplus is filtered off, gentle heating plus slow crystallisation delivers the pure, dry sample.
medium.analogy: The excess base works like a sponge left standing in a spill: it guarantees nothing acidic remains, and wringing it out afterwards, which is the filtration, leaves the floor holding only what you wanted.
medium.examPointer: When asked why the base goes in excess, answer in terms of consuming all the acid and the danger of concentrated acid during evaporation, not in terms of yield.

check.stem: Why is the insoluble base added in excess?

options.text: So that all of the acid reacts
options.explanation: Surplus base guarantees no acid survives into the evaporation stage.

options.text: To make the salt more soluble
options.explanation: Solubility is a property of the salt itself and does not change with extra base.

options.text: To speed up the filtering step
options.explanation: Extra solid gives the filter more work, not less; the reason is about the acid, not the filtering.

options.text: So the crystals grow larger
options.explanation: Crystal size depends on evaporation speed, not on leftover solid.

check.stem: What would happen if unreacted acid were left in the solution during evaporation?

options.text: It would become dangerously concentrated
options.explanation: As water leaves, any surviving acid grows stronger and more hazardous in the dish.

options.text: It would evaporate away harmlessly first
options.explanation: Acids do not simply fly off ahead of the water; they concentrate instead.

options.text: It would turn into more salt
options.explanation: There is nothing left for the acid to react with, so it stays as acid.

options.text: It would neutralise the excess base
options.explanation: Whatever base remains has already done its neutralising; the residue is acid on its own.

check.stem: How is the excess solid removed once the acid has all reacted?

options.text: By filtration
options.explanation: The undissolved base is caught by the filter paper while the solution passes through.

options.text: By evaporation
options.explanation: Evaporation removes water later; it cannot separate a solid from a solution.

options.text: By decanting into a burette
options.explanation: A burette measures volumes in titrations and plays no part in this method.

options.text: By adding more acid
options.explanation: Adding acid would undo the excess-base strategy rather than clean it up.

check.stem: When should heating stop during the evaporation stage?

options.text: When small crystals begin to appear
options.explanation: The first crystals mark the point where the solution is concentrated enough to crystallise.

options.text: When the solution starts boiling vigorously
options.explanation: Vigorous boiling is about temperature, not about the crystallisation point.

options.text: Only when every drop of water has gone
options.explanation: Heating to dryness risks decomposition of the salt and is not the method.

options.text: Before the solution is warm
options.explanation: Little water would have left, so no crystals could form at all.

check.stem: How can larger crystals be obtained?

options.text: By letting the solution evaporate slowly over several days
options.explanation: Slow water loss gives dissolved particles the time to build big, ordered crystals.

options.text: By heating the solution as fast as possible
options.explanation: Fast evaporation gives many small crystals, not large ones.

options.text: By adding extra acid at the end
options.explanation: Extra acid contaminates the product instead of improving it.

options.text: By filtering more than once
options.explanation: Repeat filtering changes nothing about how the crystals grow.

lessons.title: Copper sulfate crystals
lessons.opening: The standard example is copper(II) sulfate, made by reacting black copper(II) oxide with dilute sulfuric acid until the solid is in excess. After filtering and gentle heating, blue crystals appear, and they grow larger when the water is left to evaporate slowly. A carbonate base simply releases carbon dioxide gas instead, and a suitable metal can replace the base altogether.
keyPoints: Copper(II) sulfate is made from copper(II) oxide and dilute sulfuric acid.
The reaction of copper(II) oxide with sulfuric acid produces copper(II) sulfate solution and water.
Unreacted acid left behind would become dangerously concentrated as the water evaporates.
A carbonate base releases carbon dioxide gas into the air during the reaction.
An acid can instead be reacted with a metal above hydrogen in the reactivity series.

low.restatement: Black copper(II) oxide plus dilute sulfuric acid gives blue copper(II) sulfate solution and water. Filter, heat gently until crystals start, then leave the rest to evaporate slowly for bigger crystals.
low.analogy: The black powder vanishing into the acid is like sugar vanishing in tea: the solid seems to disappear, but it has simply joined the liquid as new blue salt.
low.examPointer: Learn the copper(II) oxide plus sulfuric acid equation, because the copper(II) sulfate preparation is the named example examiners quote.

medium.restatement: Copper(II) oxide reacts with sulfuric acid to give copper(II) sulfate and water, with no gas made. With a carbonate base the same method works but carbon dioxide escapes, and with a metal the salt forms provided the metal sits above hydrogen yet below the dangerously reactive few.
medium.analogy: Choosing the solid reactant is like choosing a courier for a parcel: oxide, carbonate and metal all deliver the salt, but each leaves a different calling card, gas or no gas, at the door.
medium.examPointer: Questions may swap the base for a metal or carbonate, so practise saying what extra product, if any, each choice produces.

check.stem: Which reagents make copper(II) sulfate by this method?

options.text: Copper(II) oxide and dilute sulfuric acid
options.explanation: Insoluble oxide plus acid is exactly the method, and sulfate comes from sulfuric acid.

options.text: Copper metal and dilute sulfuric acid
options.explanation: Copper sits below hydrogen, so it does not displace hydrogen from the acid.

options.text: Copper(II) carbonate and dilute hydrochloric acid
options.explanation: Hydrochloric acid would give the chloride, not the sulfate.

options.text: Copper(II) sulfate and water
options.explanation: The product cannot be its own starting material.

check.stem: What is observed when a carbonate base reacts with the acid?

options.text: Effervescence as carbon dioxide is released
options.explanation: Carbonates release carbon dioxide gas, which is seen as fizzing.

options.text: A colour change from blue to white
options.explanation: That is the anhydrous copper(II) sulfate water test, not this reaction.

options.text: The mixture turns alkaline
options.explanation: The acid is being neutralised, so the mixture does not turn alkaline.

options.text: Nothing, because carbonates are insoluble
options.explanation: Insoluble bases still react with acids; insolubility does not mean inertness.

check.stem: Which metal could safely be used instead of a base to make a salt from acid?

options.text: Magnesium, which sits above hydrogen but is not dangerously reactive
options.explanation: The safe window is above hydrogen yet below the metals that react explosively.

options.text: Copper, which is below hydrogen
options.explanation: Metals below hydrogen do not react with dilute acids to make salts.

options.text: Sodium, which reacts explosively
options.explanation: Too-reactive metals make the reaction dangerous rather than useful.

options.text: Gold, which is unreactive but above hydrogen
options.explanation: Gold sits below hydrogen and would do nothing in the acid.

check.stem: What are the products when copper(II) oxide reacts with dilute sulfuric acid?

options.text: Copper(II) sulfate and water
options.explanation: Acid plus metal oxide always gives salt plus water.

options.text: Copper(II) sulfite and hydrogen
options.explanation: Sulfuric acid makes sulfates, and no hydrogen is released with an oxide.
options.misconception: wrong salt family and invented gas

options.text: Copper and sulfuric acid
options.explanation: That reverses the reaction; the oxide is consumed, not produced.

options.text: Copper(II) hydroxide and sulfate
options.explanation: Those are fragments of the reactants, not the products.

check.stem: Why is the leftover solid filtered off before evaporation?

options.text: So only the salt and water remain in the solution
options.explanation: Removing the surplus base leaves a solution with nothing but the product in it.

options.text: To remove the blue colour
options.explanation: The blue colour belongs to the wanted salt, not to an impurity.

options.text: To add water of crystallisation
options.explanation: Filtration removes solid; it adds nothing to the solution.

options.text: To concentrate the acid further
options.explanation: All the acid has already reacted; there is no free acid to concentrate.

glossary.definition: A salt that dissolves in water, prepared here from an acid and an insoluble base.
More than enough of a reactant, added so the other reactant is completely used up.
Separating an undissolved solid from a liquid by passing the mixture through filter paper.
The change from liquid to vapour that concentrates a solution as it is heated.
The formation of ordered solid crystals as a concentrated solution loses water.
